title: The Ladybug’s Lost Spots
sum: Poppy the ladybug can’t see her own back, so her garden friends count her seven spots for her, and after a big rain the spots keep going missing.

cast.d: a little ladybug who can’t see her own back, so friends count her spots
cast.look: a small round ladybug with a shiny red back, seven black spots and a black head with two white patches

cast.d: an old garden snail, slow and kind, who counts Poppy’s spots every morning
cast.look: a garden snail with a brown swirly shell and eyes on the tips of two long feelers

cast.d: a robin who hunts worms after the rain
cast.look: a plump robin with an orange chest, a brown back and round black eyes

cast.d: a little green caterpillar who wishes he could fly
cast.look: a small green caterpillar with a round face and tiny legs

cast.d: a brand-new ladybug who comes out of the orange bump
cast.look: a small ladybug, pale yellow at first, then orange-red with seven black spots

p: Poppy was a little ladybug with a shiny red back. She had seven round, black spots. But Poppy had never seen them.
Her spots were on her back. She could not turn her head that far. So every morning, Moss the snail counted them for her. “Seven,” he always said.
One morning the sky turned gray. A cool wind shook the garden. Plip! A raindrop hit the path. Plop! Another one hit a rose.
To Poppy, each raindrop was as big as a beach ball. She did not want one on her head. She ran past the rose bush and under a big green leaf.
Then the rain came down hard. Plip, plop, plip, plop! The drops drummed on the leaf above her. Poppy held on tight with all six legs.
Under the leaf, it was dim and dry. Rainwater ran down to the leaf’s pointy tip. It dripped off, drop after drop, like beads on a string.
Poppy was not alone under there. A small orange bump was stuck to the leaf. It had black dots, and it did not move.
“Hello?” said Poppy. The bump said nothing. She poked it with one leg. Still nothing.
So Poppy made up a song instead. “Plip, plop, drip, drop. Rain, rain, time to stop!” She sang it once. She sang it twice.
The third time, the drumming began to slow. Plip. Plip. Then nothing at all.
The sun peeked out, and the whole garden sparkled. “It worked!” said Poppy. She crawled out into the warm light.
Down the path came Moss, wet and shiny. Snails love rain. He had been out in it all morning, and he looked very pleased.
“Count my spots, please,” said Poppy. She turned her back to him. Moss stretched out his two long feelers. His eyes sat right on the tips, like peas on sticks.
“One, two, three, four, five,” said Moss. He stopped. “Five.”
“Five?” Poppy’s antennae shot straight up. “Where are the others? The rain washed them off!”
She looked on the path. She looked in the wet grass. She even looked under the big green leaf. There were no black spots anywhere.
But there was one thing Poppy could not see. A scrap of pink rose petal was stuck to her back.
Moss leaned in close. “Hmm,” he said. “What’s this pink thing?” He gave it a push with one feeler.
The wet petal slid off and landed with a splat. Under it were the lost spots, black and round, right where they belonged.
Moss counted again, all the way to seven. “Same as always,” he said. “Spots don’t wash off. They’re part of you, like my shell.”
Poppy did a little dance on the path. Wiggle, wiggle, spin! Behind her, under the big green leaf, the orange bump sat still. Waiting.

art.s: A small red ladybug shelters under a big green leaf in the rain beside a little orange bump, while a garden snail with eyes on long feelers comes down the wet path.

q.q: Draw where Poppy hid from the rain. Show the raindrops too.
look: Raindrops falling on top of the leaf
q.e: The big leaf worked like an umbrella. Poppy stayed nice and dry!

q.q: What sound did the rain make on Poppy’s leaf?
q.e: Plip, plop! Can you say it like the rain?

q.q: Moss counted five spots. Poppy had seven. How many hid under the petal?
q.e: Five and two more make seven. Two spots were hiding under the petal.

p: The morning after the big rain, the garden smelled fresh and wet. Poppy the ladybug sat on a daisy, warming her red back.
All over the lawn, worms were coming up out of the wet ground. Wiggle, wiggle. Poppy counted three pink worms. Then a fourth one popped up.
Then a shadow fell over the daisy. Hop. Hop. Hop. A robin with an orange chest was looking for breakfast.
Poppy’s legs began to shake. Robins ate bugs. And Poppy was a bug!
She dove onto a leaf and held very still. But she was bright red on bright green. She stuck out like a strawberry on a salad.
“Why am I so red?” Poppy whispered. “Why can’t I be green, like a leaf?”
The robin hopped closer. She tipped her head and looked at Poppy with one round, black eye. Closer. Closer.
Poppy did the only thing she could think of. She squeezed a tiny yellow drop out of her knees. It smelled awful.
The robin pulled back fast. “Pee-yew!” she said. “Red and stinky. I know you bugs!”
She peered down at Poppy’s back. “Red back, black spots. Let me see. Three on this side. Three on that side.”
She tapped the air with her beak. “And one in the middle, right behind your head. Seven spots. Yep, you’re a ladybug.”
“I tasted a ladybug once, when I was a little chick,” said the robin. “Yuck! Like old socks. I spit it right out.”
The robin shook her feathers. “Now when I see red and black, I think, no thank you.” She hopped away across the lawn. Peck! She pulled up a long pink worm instead.
Poppy let out a long breath, and her legs stopped shaking. So that was what her red back was for. It was not for hiding. It was a sign that said, Don’t eat me!
Poppy climbed back to the top of the daisy. She stood up as tall as a ladybug could stand. “Red and black!” she shouted after the robin. “Stay back!”
The robin turned around. “Don’t worry,” she said, with her mouth full of worm. “I’m Rosie, by the way. Nice spots.”
Later, Moss the snail came up the daisy stem. He was late for the morning spot count. “Did I miss anything?” he asked.
“A robin counted my spots,” said Poppy. “She got seven.”
Moss looked at the lawn, then at Rosie, then at Poppy. “Well,” he said. “She can count.”

art.s: A red ladybug stands tall on a white daisy while a plump robin with an orange chest tilts its head at her, and pink worms wiggle on the wet lawn.

q.q: Draw Poppy’s back with three spots on each side and one in the middle.
look: One spot in the middle, behind her head
q.e: Three and three and one make seven, just the way Rosie counted!

q.q: Why did Rosie hop away from Poppy?
q.e: Rosie remembered the yucky taste. Poppy’s red back says, “Don’t eat me!”

q.q: When Rosie hopped close, Poppy’s legs shook. How did Poppy feel?
q.e: Shaky legs can mean scared. Soon Poppy’s legs stopped shaking.

p: Poppy the ladybug could not see her own back. So every morning, Moss the snail counted her spots. “Seven,” he always said, and Poppy always said, “Thank you.”
But today Moss was late, and Poppy was hungry. She flew to the big rose bush for lunch. Whirr!
The rose bush did not look well. Its leaves were curled up tight, like little fists. Its buds hung down.
Poppy crawled down a stem and stopped. Tiny green bugs sat all along it. They were soft and round, lined up like peas in a pod.
“Aphids!” said Poppy. The aphids did not even look up. Their mouths were poked into the stem, like straws in juice boxes. Slurp, slurp, slurp.
No wonder the rose looked so droopy. The aphids were drinking its juice. Poppy’s tummy rumbled.
She counted them first. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Ten fat aphids, all in a row.
“Munch, crunch,” sang Poppy. “Aphids for lunch!” She started at the bottom of the stem and ate her way up.
Munch, crunch, one. Munch, crunch, two. On she went, up and up the stem.
Munch, crunch, seven. Munch, crunch, eight. Munch, crunch, nine.
Poppy’s tummy was round and tight. “Oof,” she said. Where was number ten? Poppy was too full to care.
She climbed onto a leaf in the sun and closed her eyes. It was a very good spot for a nap.
Soon Moss came up the stem, slow as always. “Sorry I’m late,” he said. “Turn around. Let’s count.”
Poppy turned around. Moss stretched out his feelers. “One, two, three, four, five, six black spots,” he said. “And one green spot.”
“A green spot?” Poppy twisted to look. She turned left, then right. She spun round and round like a top.
Then the green spot got up. It walked down her side, across the leaf and back onto the stem. And there, where it had been, was Poppy’s seventh black spot!
Moss laughed so hard his shell wobbled. “Your spot has legs!” he said.
It was the last aphid. It had been riding on Poppy’s back the whole time. Now it sat on the stem and looked at her.
Poppy looked at the aphid. The aphid looked at Poppy. “Go on,” said Poppy. “I’m much too full.”
The aphid crept off down the stem, slow as a snail. “Hey,” said Moss.
Then he looked up at the droopy rose. “Nine fewer aphids,” he said. “Now it can keep its juice.”
Poppy laughed and turned around again. Moss counted all the way to seven. Seven black spots, and not one green one.

art.s: A ladybug naps on a rose leaf with one tiny green aphid sitting on her back, while an old snail stretches his feelers to count her spots.

q.q: There were ten aphids, and Poppy ate nine. How many were left?
q.e: Ten take away nine leaves one. That one rode on Poppy’s back!

q.q: Which word rhymes with “munch” in Poppy’s song?
q.e: Munch, crunch, lunch! They all end with the same sound.

q.q: Draw the aphids drinking from the rose stem. Show the curly leaves too.
look: Tiny green aphids on the stem
Poppy coming to eat the aphids
q.e: Aphids drink a plant’s juice. Ladybugs eat aphids, so ladybugs help the roses!

p: Inch was a little green caterpillar. He was new in the garden, and he ate leaves all day long. Chomp, chomp, chomp. Every leaf he sat on had holes in it.
One morning, something red zoomed over his head. Whirr! It landed right beside him. It was a ladybug with a shiny red back and black spots.
“Hi, I’m Poppy,” said the ladybug. Inch stared at her. “You can fly! How do you do it?”
Poppy thought about it. Nobody had ever asked her that. “Well,” she said. “I just go.”
“Can you go slower?” asked Inch. “So I can see?”
So Poppy showed him, one step at a time. First, she lifted her hard red covers. They opened down the middle, like two little doors.
Next, out came two thin wings. They had been folded up underneath, like a map in a pocket. The wings were so thin that Inch could see the sun through them.
Last, she flapped. Whirr! Up she went, once around the rose bush and back again.
Inch counted her spots as she zoomed past. “One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight! You have eight spots!”
Poppy landed and tucked her wings away. The red covers closed. “I have seven,” she said. “Moss the snail counts them every morning. Always seven.”
Inch counted her spots again. Seven. He wrinkled up his little green face. “Fly again,” he said.
Up went Poppy. “Eight!” shouted Inch. Down came Poppy. “Seven!” Up. “Eight!” Down. “Seven!”
At last Poppy flopped onto the leaf, out of breath. “Inch,” she puffed. “I can’t fly all day. What is going on?”
Inch crawled up close. He looked at the middle of her back, just behind her head. One round spot sat there, right on the line between her two red covers.
“Open your covers,” said Inch. “Just a tiny bit.”
Poppy lifted them a little. The middle spot split in two! One half went left, and one half went right.
“Two halves!” said Inch. “When you fly, that spot looks like two. That makes eight!” Poppy closed her covers. The halves came back together, round and whole.
“Seven on the ground,” said Poppy. “Eight in the air.” She laughed so hard that she rolled right off the leaf. Plop! She landed on a softer one below.
Inch looked at his own back. It was plain and green, with no covers at all. “I’ll never fly,” he said, and his head drooped.
“Not yet,” said Poppy. She pointed to a small orange bump under a big green leaf. “Moss says lots of little bugs make bumps like that. When the bump opens, out come wings.”
Inch looked at the bump for a long, long time. Then he went back to his leaf. Chomp, chomp, chomp. He had a lot of growing to do.

art.s: A ladybug flies with her red wing covers open and thin see-through wings spread, while a small green caterpillar on a chewed leaf counts her spots.

q.q: What did Poppy do first, to fly?
q.e: First the red covers open. Next the wings come out. Last, whirr, she flaps!

q.q: What was folded up under Poppy’s hard red covers?
q.e: Ladybugs keep their thin flying wings folded under their hard red covers.

q.q: Draw Poppy flying with her covers open. Show the middle spot in two halves.
look: The middle spot split into two halves
q.e: Three, three and two halves. It looks like eight, but it’s still seven spots!

p: A small orange bump with black dots sat under a big green leaf. Poppy the ladybug had found it on the day of the big rain. It never moved. It never said hello.
“What’s inside?” Poppy asked Moss the snail. Moss only said, “Wait and see.” Moss said that a lot.
Then, one warm morning, Poppy heard a tiny sound. Crick. Crack. The bump was splitting open at the top!
“Come quick!” Poppy called. Inch the caterpillar came, chomp, chomp, with a leaf still in his mouth. Moss came too. Well, he started to.
Out of the bump crawled a brand-new ladybug. She was soft and shiny and pale yellow, like butter. Her back had no spots at all.
“Oh no,” said Inch. “Her spots are lost!”
Poppy checked the new ladybug’s back for a stuck petal. Nothing. Just smooth, pale yellow.
The new ladybug looked up at them. “What are spots?” she asked.
At last Moss arrived. He stretched out his feelers and took a long look. “She’s brand new,” he said. “Give her the day. Wait and see.”
So they waited. The new ladybug sat in the sun to dry. Her soft back grew hard and shiny, like a tiny bowl.
By lunch, her yellow was turning orange. Little gray dots were showing through. Poppy counted them. “One, two, three, four. Four spots!”
“Four is a good start,” said Inch. They waited some more. Inch ate half a leaf, and Moss took a nap. The new ladybug tried to walk in a straight line and fell over twice.
At sunset, her back was orange-red, and the spots were black and clear. Poppy counted again, one by one, all the way to seven. “Seven!” she shouted. “Just like me!”
Poppy had never counted spots before today. She could not see her own, so Moss always counted for her. But this back she could see, every bit of it.
“You need a name,” said Poppy. “This morning you were yellow, like the sun. How about Sunny?” The new ladybug wiggled her antennae. That meant yes.
Just then, a cool wind shook the garden. Plip! Plop! “Rain!” said Poppy. “Quick, under the leaf!”
The two ladybugs sat side by side under the big green leaf. Rain drummed on top. Poppy taught Sunny her rain song. “Plip, plop, drip, drop. Rain, rain, time to stop!”
Then Sunny poked Poppy with one leg. “Turn around,” she said. “I’ll count yours.” And she did, all the way to seven.
Two ladybugs. Fourteen spots. One big green leaf, with the rain going plip, plop on top.

art.s: Two ladybugs, one bright red and one pale orange, sit side by side under a big green leaf in the rain, next to an empty orange bump.

q.q: Draw Sunny coming out of the bump. What does she say? Add a speech bubble.
look: A pale yellow ladybug with no spots
A speech bubble with her words
q.e: Maybe she said, “What are spots?” What a fun speech bubble!

q.q: Sunny had four spots at lunch and seven at sunset. How many more came?
q.e: Four, then five, six, seven. Three more spots came.

q.q: Why did Sunny have no spots at first?
q.e: New ladybugs come out pale and soft. Their color and spots show up as their backs dry and harden.

fin.q: Who counted Poppy’s spots with no mix-up at all?
fin.e: Rosie counted three, three and one. Seven, with no mix-up!

fin.q: In the very first rain, who was already under the leaf with Poppy?
fin.e: The orange bump was Sunny! She was under the leaf with Poppy all along.
